newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin plays complex power game with Lebed.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin plays complex power game with Lebed.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin is playing a complex power game with Alexander Lebed in which he is trying to keep his ambitious security chief in check but does not want to turn him into a dangerous enemy.
After weeks of hedging, Yeltsin finally came to Lebed's defence on Thursday over a controversial peace deal in Chechnya and rejected his apparent threat to quit over a minor issue.
But within hours, Yeltsin was seen on television chiding Lebed for not working closely enough with the government.

The 65-year-old president's seemingly contradictory behaviour highlighted the delicacy of his relationship with the 46-year-old former paratroop commander but also what appears to be a temporary need for one another.

"What Yeltsin is trying to do is keep Lebed in his company but not give him too much chance to show his capabilities and political weight," Viktor Kremenyuk, an analyst at the independent USA and Canada Institute thinktank, told Reuters.

"As long as he is in the administration, he is not a leader and has appropriate duties. But as soon as he leaves, he can acquire the aura of the leader of all opposition forces and weaken the position of the administration significantly."
Lebed is a potential power rival. He finished third in the presidential election in June, does not hide his presidential ambitions and has worked hard to build up a public following.

His outspoken comments and unpredictable behaviour threaten a delicate balance which Yeltsin has tried to create between rival interest groups in the Kremlin which is especially valuable while he is in hospital awaiting heart surgery.

Lebed even missed Friday's first meeting of the new Defence Council, of which he is a member, in an apparent snub of the council's secretary who has won from Lebed responsibilities for senior military appointments.
But Lebed, who won more than 11 million votes in the election, brings a measure of public support to a Kremlin administration which is unpopular in many quarters.

By squeezing Lebed too hard, Yeltsin risks driving Russia's most charismatic politician into the opposition, where he could galvanise calls for the president to quit for health reasons and stir up unrest among millions of unpaid workers.

"Mr Lebed's resignation for deep ideological reasons and his departure into the ranks of the regime's accusers could lead to the creation of a real opposition leader on a national scale," Dmitry Volkov, deputy editor of the newspaper Sevodnya, said.

Communists and other opposition parties are already calling for Yeltsin to quit, saying the country is rudderless and that decision-making has been frozen. There is a risk of widespread labour unrest if workers do not receive the wages they are owed.

The president can ill afford such problems while his ability to hit back is limited by his absence from the Kremlin. He is expected to have a heart bypass operation in about two months time and is likely to need about two months to recover.

But although many political analysts believe it is only a matter of time until Lebed jumps ship, he is not likely to leave the Kremlin of his own accord unless he is certain a new presidential election is not far off.

Lebed owes his position entirely to Yeltsin. He has been forced to give up his parliamentary seat by entering the Kremlin and has no major political party or power base on which to rely if he goes into opposition.
"Who is Lebed if he leaves now? He has no political structures behind him and no means of applying pressure," political analyst Alexander Konovalov said.

"If Lebed resigns and the president recovers from his operation, Lebed would be in a position where he had little chance to act and would risk being forgotten because elections would be a long way off," Konovalov added.
While in power, Lebed risks being associated with an unpopular government but is at least assured of a voice and plenty of media coverage to keep him in the eye of the voters.

He also has the chance to prove he is a man of action by carrying out his promises to fight crime and provide a lasting peace in breakaway Chechnya, where a ceasefire has largely held under the peace agreement which he signed on August 31.
